messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Stress: Stress, Idealized Families: Happy families
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mina was a 22-year-old married woman from a South Eastern Asian family who had been working as a call center agent when she first described how the assault had altered ordinary life for her. The assault itself had happened quickly and without warning, in a setting that should have felt routine rather than dangerous, and what stayed with her most was not a single clear narrative but a series of disconnected pieces: the sudden shift in tone, the sense of being trapped, and, later, the way certain sensory details returned more sharply than the rest. When the memory came back, she said it did not feel like an ordinary recollection at all; it felt more real and vivid than the everyday events of her current life, as if she were back inside it rather than thinking about it from a distance. One of the details that returned with particular force was taste. She could taste what she had tasted during the event when the memory surfaced, and this made the memory feel immediate and bodily in a way that unsettled her. Because the pieces did not fit together into a clean sequence, she found herself repeatedly trying and failing to line them up into something coherent, and the fragments returned without warning.

In the weeks and months that followed, Mina began noticing that certain situations carried a charge that she could feel before she could explain it. Ambulances were especially distressing. If one passed outside her apartment or came through the neighborhood while she was at work, the sound alone could pull her attention away from the call in her headset and make her go still. Stress in any form had a similar effect; busy shifts, pressure from supervisors, or even the ordinary strain of a crowded day could make her feel abruptly more exposed. She also found herself unsettled by happy families, particularly when she saw them together in public or in advertisements on the screen at home. Those images of ease and closeness did not feel comforting to her. Instead, they intensified her sense of being separate from a kind of safety she could see but not enter, and she would look away quickly or turn the channel.

Mina had come to avoid reminders whenever she could, especially when others brought up anything that echoed the assault. If someone mentioned a related topic directly, she would become tense and change the subject, or excuse herself and go quiet. She also noticed that she used sexual fantasies and activities to release tension, describing this not as pleasure so much as something she turned to when the pressure in her body felt too high to hold. At the same time, she avoided authority figures and anyone in uniform. In practical terms, this showed up at work and in the community. On her commute and in the building where she lived, she became acutely uncomfortable around security guards, police officers, and other uniformed people. At work, when supervisors approached her desk, she felt a strong urge to shrink inward and keep the interaction brief. She did not frame this as rebellion; rather, she felt that being near people in authority left her too alert, too watched, and too vulnerable.

Her sense of threat remained active in the ordinary flow of the day. Mina scanned exits as soon as she entered any room or building, automatically noting doors, hallways, and the fastest way out. In the call center, she did this without meaning to the moment she walked onto the floor, checking the nearest exits before settling into her station. She also constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger, reading the body language of people around her and tracking movement at the edge of her awareness. Unexpected movement nearby caused her to react as if she were in danger; if a coworker stepped behind her or a customer in the lobby shifted suddenly, she jerked and felt her heart race before she had time to tell herself she was safe. She had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, and this conviction was not abstract for her. It shaped how she sat, where she looked, and how much of herself she allowed into a room.

Mina also described an enduring belief that she was inadequate. She did not present this as self-pity, but as a settled judgment about herself that had become part of the way she interpreted her own reactions and limitations. There were moments when she looked at how much she had withdrawn or how quickly she now became tense, and she concluded that she was not coping the way she should. She was especially troubled by the thought that if she let herself think about the assault directly, she would not be able to handle it. That belief made her avoid the memory whenever possible, even though it continued to intrude in fragments and sensations. Over time, her efforts to keep the subject away from conversation made her feel more isolated from others, including her husband, who wanted to help but did not always know how to approach the topic without upsetting her.

By the time she sought help, Mina was worn down by the constant effort of staying alert, changing the subject, and orienting herself toward exits and uniforms whenever she left the house. She came in saying that she no longer wanted to keep living as if danger were waiting in every room, and she was most afraid that if she tried to face what had happened, she would fall apart. At the same time, she was hoping that she might learn how to think about the assault without being overwhelmed by the vivid fragments, the taste that returned with them, and the sense that her body was still bracing for something that had already passed.
